title: Attachment, Love & Relationship Patterns
description: Start with two introductory modules on the essential ideas and how to reason from evidence. Then practise applying the ideas in a detailed case.

nodes.title: Start here
nodes.body:
Attachment theory tries to explain how experiences of closeness and reliability shape our expectations of others. The point is to understand a pattern of relating, not to hand people an identity label.

What do we expect when an important person is unavailable?
nodes.sources: Bowlby (1982), Attachment and Loss; Mikulincer & Shaver (2016), Attachment in Adulthood.

nodes.title: What attachment expectation means
nodes.body:
A learned prediction about whether someone important will be available when we need them.

For example: A delayed reply feels unusually threatening because someone expects closeness to disappear.

One important limit: An expectation can be influenced by what this particular person has actually done.
nodes.sources: Bowlby (1982), Attachment and Loss; Mikulincer & Shaver (2016), Attachment in Adulthood.

nodes.title: Find the first concept
nodes.prompt: Consider this example: A delayed reply feels unusually threatening because someone expects closeness to disappear. Which concept is most directly demonstrated, without claiming anything beyond the example?
nodes.explanation: The example most directly supports attachment expectation. A learned prediction about whether someone important will be available when we need them. An expectation can be influenced by what this particular person has actually done.
nodes.counterexample: Attachment patterns are probabilistic models shaped by experience and context, not fixed identities derived from a single unanswered message.
nodes.sources: Bowlby (1982), Attachment and Loss; Mikulincer & Shaver (2016), Attachment in Adulthood.

nodes.title: What reassurance seeking means
nodes.body:
Asking for signs that the relationship is secure when uncertainty feels difficult.

For example: Someone sends several messages asking whether everything is okay after a long silence.

One important limit: Reassurance can help; its effects depend on how the need and response develop over time.
nodes.sources: Bowlby (1982), Attachment and Loss; Mikulincer & Shaver (2016), Attachment in Adulthood.

nodes.title: What availability means
nodes.body:
Whether another person is realistically able and willing to respond when support is needed.

For example: A partner cannot reply during a shift but offers a reliable time to speak afterwards.

One important limit: Being unavailable for a few hours is not necessarily being emotionally unreliable.
nodes.sources: Bowlby (1982), Attachment and Loss; Mikulincer & Shaver (2016), Attachment in Adulthood.

nodes.title: What working model means
nodes.body:
A changeable set of expectations formed through experience of relationships.

For example: A person anticipates rejection even when a new friend has usually been reliable.

One important limit: A working model is not a fixed diagnosis or an explanation that overrides current evidence.
nodes.sources: Bowlby (1982), Attachment and Loss; Mikulincer & Shaver (2016), Attachment in Adulthood.

lessons.title: First notice what happened
lessons.teach: Read what is said before deciding why anyone said it.
lessons.objective: Apply foundations to observable evidence, uncertainty and proportional decisions.

nodes.title: A situation, not a diagnosis
nodes.body:
Nina and Eli have been dating for six months. Eli usually replies during lunch, but today his phone is off while he is travelling.

You can describe an event accurately while remaining uncertain about why it happened.
nodes.sources: Bowlby (1982), Attachment and Loss; Mikulincer & Shaver (2016), Attachment in Adulthood.

nodes.title: Listen before you interpret
nodes.prompt: Follow the four messages. Keep the difference between the words said and their possible meaning in mind.
nodes.explanation: The purpose is to connect the term to what can actually be observed.
nodes.counterexample: Attachment patterns are probabilistic models shaped by experience and context, not fixed identities derived from a single unanswered message.
nodes.sources: Bowlby (1982), Attachment and Loss; Mikulincer & Shaver (2016), Attachment in Adulthood.
nodes.scenario: Nina and Eli have been dating for six months. Eli usually replies during lunch, but today his phone is off while he is travelling.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: You haven't replied since this morning. Are we okay?

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: My phone died on the train. I only just saw your messages.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I knew there could be a reason, but I kept thinking something had changed.

checks.prompt: What is the most careful conclusion we can draw from the exchange so far?

options.label: We can describe what each speaker requested, while treating any account of their motives as provisional.
options.feedback: This keeps the distinction between what was said and why it may have been said. The latter requires more evidence.

options.label: We can take the last speaker’s explanation as the main cause, because it is the latest information.
options.feedback: Order of speaking does not determine evidential quality; the earlier words still matter.

options.label: We can give the two speakers’ interpretations equal weight, regardless of which one fits the details.
options.feedback: Plausible alternatives can receive different weights when the observed details support them differently.

options.label: We can infer that one speaker has a stable psychological trait if their response appears defensive.
options.feedback: A single interaction may reflect a situation rather than a trait that persists across settings.

options.label: We can stop analysing the situation because multiple explanations remain logically possible.
options.feedback: Uncertainty is a reason to test explanations, not to abandon reasoning.

checks.explanation: People can be sincere about their experience and still have incomplete explanations of why events happened. Attachment patterns are probabilistic models shaped by experience and context, not fixed identities derived from a single unanswered message.
checks.counterexample: Attachment patterns are probabilistic models shaped by experience and context, not fixed identities derived from a single unanswered message.

nodes.title: A description or an assumption?
nodes.prompt: Does the sentence report something we can check, or interpret what it might mean?
nodes.explanation: The spoken words are evidence about what was said. A theory of why somebody said them is an interpretation that may need testing.
nodes.counterexample: Attachment patterns are probabilistic models shaped by experience and context, not fixed identities derived from a single unanswered message.
nodes.sources: Bowlby (1982), Attachment and Loss; Mikulincer & Shaver (2016), Attachment in Adulthood.

items.label: “You haven't replied since this morning. Are we okay?”
A temporary absence of contact is being interpreted through an expectation about relational availability. Attachment-related expectations can guide what a person notices and how they respond.
“My phone died on the train. I only just saw your messages.”
Nina may have recently experienced broken promises from Eli, in which case concern about his reliability could reflect current evidence.

nodes.title: Why the distinction matters
nodes.body:
Nina may have recently experienced broken promises from Eli, in which case concern about his reliability could reflect current evidence.

Attachment patterns are probabilistic models shaped by experience and context, not fixed identities derived from a single unanswered message.
nodes.sources: Bowlby (1982), Attachment and Loss; Mikulincer & Shaver (2016), Attachment in Adulthood.

lessons.title: Two explanations can sound reasonable
lessons.teach: Evidence should be able to change which explanation you prefer.
lessons.objective: Apply foundations to observable evidence, uncertainty and proportional decisions.

nodes.title: Start with competing accounts
nodes.body:
A temporary absence of contact is being interpreted through an expectation about relational availability. Attachment-related expectations can guide what a person notices and how they respond.

Another possibility: Nina may have recently experienced broken promises from Eli, in which case concern about his reliability could reflect current evidence.
nodes.sources: Bowlby (1982), Attachment and Loss; Mikulincer & Shaver (2016), Attachment in Adulthood.

nodes.title: What should we find out?
nodes.prompt: Both interpretations are plausible. What would actually help choose between them?
nodes.explanation: Compare Nina's responses across relationships and circumstances, and examine Eli's actual communication history. The question is what would change our view, rather than what would merely confirm it.
nodes.counterexample: Attachment patterns are probabilistic models shaped by experience and context, not fixed identities derived from a single unanswered message.
nodes.sources: Bowlby (1982), Attachment and Loss; Mikulincer & Shaver (2016), Attachment in Adulthood.

options.label: Ask the speakers how intense their feelings were and use the stronger reaction to identify the main cause.
options.feedback: The strength of a feeling does not establish its cause.

options.label: Ask for a longer account from the speaker who was most upset, since they experienced the largest impact.
options.feedback: The account matters, but the amount of distress is not a direct test of someone else’s motive.

options.label: Compare Nina's responses across relationships and circumstances, and examine Eli's actual communication history.
options.feedback: This observation could make a meaningful difference between the competing explanations.

options.label: Find a second argument and see whether it sounds similar without comparing what changed.
options.feedback: A similar argument can occur for different reasons; comparison requires the relevant circumstances.

options.label: Ask an uninvolved friend to guess which personality type best describes the speaker.
options.feedback: A personality guess is less useful than identifying a testable difference between the proposed processes.

nodes.title: Something new has been found
nodes.body: The previous week Eli had cancelled twice without explanation and then avoided a discussion about it.
nodes.sources: Bowlby (1982), Attachment and Loss; Mikulincer & Shaver (2016), Attachment in Adulthood.

nodes.title: Revise your view
nodes.prompt: Which response to this new information is justified?
nodes.explanation: The new context makes present-day reliability a stronger part of the explanation. Nina's reaction need not be attributed entirely to an enduring attachment tendency.
nodes.counterexample: Attachment patterns are probabilistic models shaped by experience and context, not fixed identities derived from a single unanswered message.
nodes.sources: Bowlby (1982), Attachment and Loss; Mikulincer & Shaver (2016), Attachment in Adulthood.

options.label: Keep the original explanation because it initially fitted the facts.
options.feedback: A reasonable earlier account can be revised as new evidence appears.

options.label: Prefer the explanation that most closely matches the new detail, while keeping other plausible causes open.
options.feedback: This revises confidence in response to information rather than to the apparent sophistication of the theory.

options.label: Treat the new evidence as decisive proof of a single hidden intention.
options.feedback: The evidence can favour an account without establishing complete access to another person’s motives.

options.label: Give every explanation identical weight because certainty is impossible.
options.feedback: Uncertainty does not require all accounts to be equally likely.

options.label: Ignore the new detail until each speaker independently agrees on its meaning.
options.feedback: Agreement may help cooperation, but it is not a prerequisite for evaluating evidence.

lessons.title: Ready for a real case
lessons.teach: You have the concepts. Now practise using them without jumping beyond the evidence.
lessons.objective: Apply foundations to observable evidence, uncertainty and proportional decisions.

lessons.title: When silence feels like distance
lessons.teach: Follow the conversation one message at a time. Notice what the behaviour might be achieving before you decide why it happened. About five minutes.
lessons.objective: Distinguish observable evidence from a tentative explanation of what attachment theory can explain.

nodes.title: Watch the conversation
nodes.prompt: Read the exchange one message at a time, then work from what the characters actually said.
nodes.sources: Mikulincer & Shaver, Attachment in Adulthood (2016).
nodes.scenario: Jamie cannot use a phone during an eight-hour work shift. Sofia has been checking the online status.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I started worrying when you didn't answer.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: I told you I'd be at work until eight.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I know. I kept checking whether you were online anyway.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: What would a reply have told you?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: That we're okay. Every time I checked and saw nothing, I felt worse.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: I want us to be close, but I can't keep a phone with me during work.

checks.prompt: Which psychological interpretation is currently best supported?

options.label: Sofia may be treating delayed contact as a signal about the security of the relationship.
Jamie may have broken an established agreement to check in during the shift.
Sofia may be mainly frustrated about incompatible preferences for everyday messaging.
Sofia may be using the online indicator to test whether Jamie has changed his usual communication routine.
options.feedback: A changed routine would matter, but Jamie has already explained the shift restriction.

options.label: Sofia may be repeating a habitual phone check because the delay is inconvenient, even without a fear about the relationship.
options.feedback: A habit could contribute, although her words about needing to know they are okay favour a closeness-related account.

checks.explanation: The strongest clues are the character's own words. Sofia may be treating delayed contact as a signal about the security of the relationship. Jamie may have broken an established agreement to check in during the shift. remains a legitimate rival, so this is a working account rather than a conclusion about personality.
checks.counterexample: Sometimes delayed replies really do signal unreliable communication. The relevant evidence includes what the couple agreed and how often expectations are unmet.

checks.prompt: You are Sofia. Which response best addresses the practical problem at this point?

options.label: Could we settle a time to speak after your shift and review whether that feels predictable enough for both of us?
options.reply: Did it make you feel secure?
options.consequence: A realistic routine could help; it does not establish that reassurance alone resolves the worry.
options.feedback: A realistic routine could help; it does not establish that reassurance alone resolves the worry.

options.label: Could we agree on when we'll catch up after shifts instead of expecting replies during work?
options.reply: Could we try having a fixed time to talk after work?
options.consequence: The conversation may not be solved, but the immediate problem now has a concrete route forward.

options.label: Would you be willing to tell me in advance when your phone will be unavailable, while I work on what I assume during the silence?
options.reply: Did it make you feel secure?

nodes.title: A new situation
nodes.body:
A friend cancels one arrangement because of illness. Another friend interprets the cancellation as a sign that the friendship is fading.

Decide what you can infer from this example without assuming the same explanation must apply.

nodes.title: An idea worth carrying forward
nodes.body:
A temporary absence of contact is being interpreted through an expectation about relational availability. Attachment-related expectations can guide what a person notices and how they respond.

Attachment patterns are probabilistic models shaped by experience and context, not fixed identities derived from a single unanswered message.

The purpose of the exercise is to make a better-supported judgement and choose a proportionate next step.

glossary.definition: A learned prediction about whether someone important will be available when we need them.
glossary.example: A delayed reply feels unusually threatening because someone expects closeness to disappear.
glossary.limit: An expectation can be influenced by what this particular person has actually done.

glossary.definition: Asking for signs that the relationship is secure when uncertainty feels difficult.
glossary.example: Someone sends several messages asking whether everything is okay after a long silence.
glossary.limit: Reassurance can help; its effects depend on how the need and response develop over time.

glossary.definition: Whether another person is realistically able and willing to respond when support is needed.
glossary.example: A partner cannot reply during a shift but offers a reliable time to speak afterwards.
glossary.limit: Being unavailable for a few hours is not necessarily being emotionally unreliable.

glossary.definition: A changeable set of expectations formed through experience of relationships.
glossary.example: A person anticipates rejection even when a new friend has usually been reliable.
glossary.limit: A working model is not a fixed diagnosis or an explanation that overrides current evidence.
